title: IBM releases SOTA Granite Time Series PatchTST-FM-r2 model with commercial-friendly license
gist: IBM Research released Granite Time Series PatchTST-FM-r2, a ~385M-parameter zero-shot time-series forecasting model that ranks #2 overall (and #1 among permissively-licensed models) on the GIFT-Eval benchmark as of September 8, 2026, released under a dual Apache-2.0/OpenMDW-1.0 license with full weights, code, and a documented pretraining corpus, and positioned for both standalone use and streaming inference via an IBM-Confluent Cloud integration.

insights.claim: As of September 8, 2026, IBM's Granite Time Series PatchTST-FM-r2 ranks #2 overall by both CRPS and MASE among replicable, zero-shot, non-leaked models on the GIFT-Eval time-series forecasting leaderboard, and is the top-ranked model in that category among models released under a permissive, commercial-friendly open-source license.
insights.speaker: Roman Vaculin
insights.so_what: Establishes IBM as currently holding the best openly-licensed zero-shot time-series forecasting model on a major public benchmark, a concrete competitive marker versus proprietary or restrictively-licensed rivals for enterprises picking a forecasting foundation model.
insights.locator: As of September 8, 2026, the model is the top performing zero-shot model

insights.claim: PatchTST-FM-r2 achieves a geometric-mean CRPS of 0.467 on GIFT-Eval among replicable zero-shot models, placing it immediately behind Google's TimesFM-3 and ahead of all other permissively-licensed competitors in that comparison.
insights.speaker: Roman Vaculin
insights.so_what: Names IBM's specific benchmark rival (TimesFM-3) and the exact score gap, giving investors a concrete metric to track in future GIFT-Eval leaderboard updates.
insights.quote: PatchTST-FM-r2 achieves a geometric-mean CRPS of 0.467, placing it immediately behind TimesFM-3 in this comparison, and first among the models with permissive licenses.

insights.claim: Even when pretrained models that were allowed to include GIFT-Eval's own evaluation-dataset training portions in their pretraining corpora are added to the comparison, PatchTST-FM-r2 still ranks 3rd for CRPS and 4th for MASE among replicable models, and outperforms several larger pretrained models including Chronos-2, Timer-S1, and Toto variants.
insights.speaker: Roman Vaculin
insights.so_what: Suggests PatchTST-FM-r2's ranking is not merely an artifact of a smaller, more selective comparison set — it remains competitive even against models with a data-leakage advantage and larger parameter counts, strengthening the architecture's claimed efficiency story.
insights.locator: Competitive even against models allowed to use benchmark training data

themes.theme: Architecture: conformer blocks over plain transformers

insights.claim: PatchTST-FM-r2's core architectural change from its predecessor PatchTST-FM-r1 is replacing standard transformer blocks with 'conformer' blocks (an architecture borrowed from speech processing) that combine multi-head self-attention with temporal convolution inside two half-step feed-forward layers, giving the model complementary long-range (attention) and local (convolution) temporal reasoning.
insights.speaker: Roman Vaculin
insights.so_what: A concrete architectural technique (conformer blocks) that investors/engineers evaluating time-series foundation models should watch for as it spreads from speech to time-series and possibly other domains.

insights.claim: The model uses ~385M parameters, supports context lengths up to 8,192 time steps, uses 50% overlapping patches with Hamming-window weighting and overlap-and-add forecasting to smooth patch-boundary artifacts, alternates convolution kernel sizes in a repeating {5,5,3,3} pattern, and expands from 20 blocks in r1 to 30 blocks in r2, while producing probabilistic forecasts via a 99-quantile prediction head.
insights.speaker: Roman Vaculin
insights.so_what: Gives a precise technical spec sheet (param count, context length, block count, quantile head) for comparing PatchTST-FM-r2's compute footprint and forecast granularity against competing time-series foundation models.

insights.claim: IBM documents PatchTST-FM-r2's pretraining corpus as consisting of four named sources — selected GiftEvalPretrain datasets, custom KernelSynth-derived synthetic data, a TSMixup corpus explicitly restricted to exclude GIFT-Eval evaluation datasets, and roughly 500,000 synthetic CauKer sequences of length 4,096 — and frames this documentation as enabling enterprise users to check for benchmark-data leakage themselves rather than trusting an opaque corpus.
insights.speaker: Roman Vaculin
insights.so_what: Positions training-data transparency (not just leaderboard score) as a criterion enterprise buyers should weigh when selecting a foundation model, and as a point of differentiation IBM is explicitly marketing versus less transparent competitors.
insights.quote: For enterprise adopters, this kind of transparency can be as important as another few points on a leaderboard.

insights.claim: Granite Time Series PatchTST-FM-r2 is dual-licensed under Apache 2.0 and OpenMDW 1.0 (the Linux Foundation's AI-model-specific license), letting users pick whichever license best suits their use case, with full model weights, architecture, inference pipeline, and benchmark-reproduction code released and made backward-compatible with existing PatchTST-FM-r1 checkpoints.
insights.speaker: Roman Vaculin
insights.so_what: A concrete, low-friction licensing and migration path (backward-compatible checkpoints, dual permissive license) that lowers switching costs for existing Granite TSFM adopters and widens commercial adoption relative to more restrictively licensed rivals.
insights.locator: Open for research experimentation — and for commercial use

insights.claim: IBM and Confluent have made several Granite Time Series models — PatchTST-FM-r1, FlowState-r1.1, TTM-r3, and TSPulse — available through an Early Access program on Confluent Cloud, running foundation-model inference directly inside Apache Flink so forecasts and anomaly-detection results can be generated from live streaming data rather than requiring a separate batch ML pipeline.
insights.speaker: Roman Vaculin
insights.so_what: Signals IBM's go-to-market strategy is embedding Granite Time Series models into existing enterprise streaming-data infrastructure (via Confluent/Flink) rather than relying solely on standalone model downloads — worth tracking as a distribution channel and potential Confluent partnership deepening.
insights.locator: From notebooks to streaming time series
